# How many words for a 60 second script? Time it to your own pace

Ask how many words fit in a 60 second script and you will often see "about 150" suggested. Treat that as a rough starting estimate, not a rule. It assumes one steady speaking pace, and the pace that matters is yours.

Some people speak quickly and clip their pauses. Others slow down for anything technical, or when reading from a prompter for the first time. A script that fits a minute for one creator can run well over for another. So the better question is: how many words do you say in a minute, with this kind of script?

## Measure your own speaking pace

This takes about two minutes and gives you a number you can keep using.

1. Take a script you have already written, or a paragraph from an old caption. Aim for 150 to 250 words.
2. Count the words. Most notes apps and word processors will do it for you.
3. Start a stopwatch and read it aloud at the pace you would use on camera. Not your rehearsal mumble, and not your nervous sprint.
4. Divide the word count by the seconds it took, then multiply by 60.

If 200 words took 85 seconds, your pace is 200 ÷ 85 × 60, or about 141 words per minute.

Do it twice, once with a casual script and once with something more detailed. If you slow down for steps, names and numbers, the second figure will be lower. Keep both.

## Turn your pace into a word budget

Once you know your pace, the maths is simple:

```text
words = your pace × seconds ÷ 60
```

Then take off a little for the parts of a video that are not words. A pause after your hook, a beat while you hold something up to the camera, a breath before the call to action. Taking off around 10 per cent is a reasonable buffer for short videos with a few deliberate pauses. If you plan to demonstrate something on screen, leave more.

For someone speaking at 140 words per minute, the budget looks like this:

- **30 seconds:** 70 words, so plan for about 60 to 65.
- **60 seconds:** 140 words, so plan for about 125.
- **90 seconds:** 210 words, so plan for about 190.
- **3 minutes:** 420 words, so plan for about 380.

These are targets for your first draft, not hard limits. The stopwatch makes the final call.

## A worked example: cutting a script to fit a minute

Say you are filming a 60 second Reel on how to clean a cast iron pan after cooking. Your pace is 140 words per minute, so your budget is around 125 words. Your first draft reads naturally but comes in at 182 words. That is roughly 78 seconds before any pauses.

Here is the opening paragraph of that draft:

> So a lot of people ask me about how to clean cast iron, and honestly I think there's a lot of confusion out there, so in this video I'm going to walk you through exactly what I do after I cook, step by step, so you never have to worry about rust again.

That is 53 words, and none of them teach anything yet. The hook is buried in the middle, and "so" appears three times. Here is the same opening after trimming:

> Cast iron pan after dinner? Here's how to clean it in four quick steps so it stays seasoned.

Now it is 18 words, and the promise comes first. That one cut saves 35 words, or about 15 seconds at this pace.

The rest of the trim tends to come from the same few places:

- **Throat clearing.** "In this video" and "so basically" fill time without moving anything forward.
- **Doubled steps.** If you say "rinse it with hot water" and then "make sure the water is hot", keep one.
- **Explanations the camera can show.** If viewers will see you wipe the pan dry, you do not need to describe the towel.
- **A long sign-off.** In a minute-long video, one clear next step is plenty.

If your revised draft is 128 words, at 140 words per minute that is about 55 seconds of speech, which leaves a few seconds for pauses. A timed read will tell you whether it really fits.

## Check the time by reading aloud, not by counting

Word counts are a planning tool. The real test is a timed read, standing or sitting the way you will film, at your filming pace.

Read it through twice. If both reads run long, cut more. If only one fits, you were probably rushing. Listen for where you sped up, because that is often a line too dense to say comfortably. Split it into two shorter sentences rather than talking faster.

Platform limits are worth checking before you record, because they change. If you are filming for a specific maximum length, aim a few seconds under it. That leaves room for the edit, a fade at the end or a line you deliver more slowly on the day.

## When a minute is the wrong length

Sometimes timing shows you something more useful than a word count: the idea does not fit. If you are cutting the steps that make the tip work, stop cutting and split it instead. "Cleaning cast iron after cooking" and "fixing rust on cast iron" are two separate videos, and each can be done well in a minute.

For help with the writing itself, the guide on [how to write a teleprompter script](/blog/how-to-write-a-teleprompter-script/) covers drafting by speaking and editing for breath. When you are ready to film, [reading a teleprompter naturally](/blog/how-to-read-a-teleprompter-naturally/) and this [talking head video setup](/blog/talking-head-video-setup/) cover the delivery and the shot.

# How to read a teleprompter without looking like you are reading

Viewers can usually tell when someone is reading. The eyes drift, the voice flattens and the pace stays oddly even. Most of this comes down to setup and habit, not talent. Here is how to read a teleprompter naturally, from where you put the words to what to do when you fluff a line.

## Keep the words close to the lens

When your eyes sit noticeably off the lens, viewers feel it. The closer your words are to the lens, the more it looks like you are talking to them. There are two common approaches, and they work differently.

**A separate reader near your filming phone.** You film on one phone and display your script on a second phone or tablet placed just below it. Keep the reading area at the very top of the reader screen, so your next words sit as close to the lens as possible. This is simple and portable. Your eyeline will be slightly below the lens, so the closer the two devices sit, the better.

**A specialist mirror rig.** A reflector rig places angled glass in front of the camera lens. The script shows on a screen beneath it and reflects in the glass, so the words appear over the lens while the camera films through the glass. Because the reflection reverses the text, the display needs to show it mirrored. These rigs give a more direct eyeline but take more setting up. Test the placement and orientation with your actual equipment before you record.

Whichever you use, a little more distance between you and the camera tends to make small eye movements less obvious. Try a few positions and watch the playback.

## Make the layout easy to scan

A wide block of small text forces your eyes to sweep across the screen. A narrow column of larger text keeps them still. Compare the same line in two layouts:

```text
Today I'm going to show you three ways to make your kitchen lighting work better on camera.
```

```text
Today I'm going to show you
three ways to make
your kitchen lighting
work better on camera.
```

The second keeps your eyes in a small area. To get there:

- Narrow the reading width.
- Increase the text size until it is comfortable from your filming position.
- Choose strong contrast between text and background for the light in your room.
- Keep only a line or two in focus, so you always know where you are.

## Let the pace follow you

Racing the scroll is one of the quickest ways to sound like you are reading. If you use timed scrolling, start slower than feels natural and speed up only once you are comfortable. You need room to pause, breathe and look up.

If your prompter can follow your voice, it moves when you speak and waits when you stop, which makes deliberate pauses easier. Either way, rehearse at the speed you will film at, not a quicker "just checking" pace.

## Bring the expression back

Reading tends to strip out the rise and fall of normal speech. A few habits help put it back:

- **Know the script well enough to glance.** The prompter is a safety net, not something to decode word by word.
- **Picture one person.** Talk to a friend who asked you the question, not to "everyone watching".
- **Mark the moments that matter.** A note for a smile, a pause or a stressed word reminds you to vary your delivery.
- **Read slightly ahead.** Taking in the next phrase before you say it lets you deliver it as a thought, not a string of words.
- **Let yourself move.** If you would gesture in conversation, do it here too.

## Recover from mistakes without restarting

Everyone stumbles. What matters is how easy the take is to fix later.

1. **Small slip? Keep going.** A tiny wobble often sounds more human than a perfect read.
2. **Bigger mistake? Pause, then restart the sentence.** Stop, breathe and say the whole sentence again from the beginning. That gives you a clean cut point in the edit.
3. **Keep the camera rolling.** Stopping for every error breaks your rhythm. Fix it in the edit instead.
4. **Lost your place?** Look to the top of the reading area, find the line and pick up from the start of that sentence.

Note the lines that keep tripping you up. Rewording them usually works better than another ten takes.

# How to write a teleprompter script that sounds like you

A teleprompter can help you sound clear and confident. It can also make you sound like you are reading the terms and conditions. The difference is rarely the device. It is the script. Most stiff scripts were written to be read silently, then spoken aloud.

## Start by talking, not typing

Before you open a blank document, say your idea out loud. Explain it as if a friend has just asked you about it. Record yourself with a voice memo app and play it back.

You will hear phrases, rhythms and examples you would never think to type. Transcribe the best parts. That rough transcript is a better first draft than anything written from scratch, because it already sounds like you.

Then answer three questions in one line each:

- Who is this video for?
- What is the one thing they should know or do by the end?
- What would you say first if they asked you in person?

If you cannot answer the second question in a sentence, the script will wander. Fix that before writing anything else.

## Write for the ear

A spoken sentence needs to be easy to follow on the first listen.

- **Keep sentences short.** One idea each.
- **Use contractions.** "You're" and "don't" sound like speech. "You are" and "do not" sound like a letter.
- **Choose the words you actually say.** "Use", not "utilise". "Help", not "facilitate".
- **Add signposts.** "Here's the thing." "Step two." They help viewers keep up.
- **Write numbers as you say them.** "Ten to fifteen minutes" is easier to read aloud than "10-15 mins".

## A before and after example

Here is a script for a short Reel about batch filming, first written like an article.

**Before**

> Batch filming is a content production method whereby creators record multiple videos in a single session, thereby maximising efficiency and ensuring consistency. It is recommended that scripts are prepared in advance, that consistent attire is utilised, and that sufficient time is allocated for setup, which can otherwise represent a significant proportion of total production time.

Every word is correct. Almost nobody talks like that.

**After**

> Want to film a week of videos in one afternoon?
>
> That's batch filming. You set up once, then record several videos back to back.
>
> Here's how to make it work.
>
> Write all your scripts first. Not on the day. Before. [pause]
>
> Wear the same top, or bring a couple of changes.
>
> And give yourself time to set up. Setting up is the slow bit. Do it once, and every video after that is quicker.

What changed:

- It opens with a question the viewer might already be asking.
- Long sentences became short ones, one idea per line.
- Formal words such as "utilised" and "allocated" became everyday ones.
- Passive phrasing became "you", speaking to one person.
- A pause is marked where the point needs a moment to land.

## Edit for breath

Now read the new version aloud at your normal speaking pace. Wherever you run short of air or rush to finish, the line is too long.

- **One breath per line or short paragraph.** Line breaks become natural pauses when you read from a prompter.
- **Mark pauses on purpose.** A blank line or a note such as [pause] reminds you to stop rather than race on.
- **Emphasise sparingly.** One stressed word per section is plenty. Mark too many and nothing stands out.
- **Swap words you trip over.** If you stumble on "particularly" every time, use "especially" or cut it.
- **Cut warm-up lines.** "In this video I'm going to talk about..." usually adds nothing.

Keep a little of your natural style, though. If you genuinely say "right, so" before a new point, leave one in. That is part of what makes it sound like you.

## Rehearsal checklist

Before you film, run through this list:

1. Read the script aloud twice, away from the camera.
2. Mark every line you stumbled on and rewrite it.
3. Check that the first sentence gives the viewer a reason to keep watching.
4. Check that each line fits in one comfortable breath.
5. Load the script onto your prompter at the text size and speed you plan to use.
6. Do one full run without stopping, even if you make mistakes.
7. Record a rehearsal and listen back. Does it sound like you talking, or you reading?
8. Read the opening and closing lines once more. They set the tone and send people off.

# A simple talking head video setup for solo creators

When you film yourself, you are also the camera operator, the sound recordist and the lighting crew. That is a lot to juggle, so the best talking head video setup is one you can repeat without thinking.

This guide gives you a six-step process: message, frame, light, audio, takes and review. Follow it the same way each time and setting up will get quicker.

## 1. Message: decide what this video is for

Before you touch the camera, finish this sentence: "This video helps [who] to [do what]." Then decide:

- **Vertical or horizontal?** This shapes every framing decision that follows.
- **Will you add text or captions in the edit?** If so, leave space for them in the frame.
- **How many videos are you filming today?** If they share a setup, film them in one session.

## 2. Frame: set the shot once, then mark it

- **Put the lens at eye level.** A camera looking up or down at you changes how you come across. Raise the phone, not your chin.
- **Place your eyes roughly a third of the way down the frame.** Leave a little room above your head, not a large gap.
- **Move a step or two away from the wall.** This reduces shadows behind you and makes the background look less flat.
- **Tidy the background.** Look for anything that pulls attention, such as a bright lamp, a cluttered shelf or a plant that seems to grow out of your head.

Once the shot looks right, mark it. Put a small piece of tape on the floor where you sit or stand, note the height of your stand and take a quick photo of the whole setup. Use those notes to rebuild the shot next time.

## 3. Light: face the light

The simplest reliable approach is to face a window, or angle your main light towards your face from slightly to one side.

- **Avoid a bright window behind you.** It can leave your face too dark.
- **Be wary of overhead light on its own.** It can leave dark shadows under your eyes.
- **Watch for mixed light.** Daylight from one side and a warm lamp from the other can give your skin two different colours.
- **Remember daylight moves.** If you rely on a window, film at a similar time each session and check the shot between videos.

If your camera app lets you lock focus and exposure, do it once you are in position, so the image does not shift when you move your hands.

## 4. Audio: get the microphone close

Clear sound matters as much as a clear picture, and it is harder to fix later. Move the microphone close enough for clear speech, but listen for popping, clothing rustle and distortion.

- **Choose the quietest room you can.** Curtains, rugs and soft furniture all help reduce echo.
- **Remove background noise.** Close windows, turn off fans and silence notifications, including on the filming phone.
- **Record a test and listen on headphones.** You will catch hum or echo that you miss while talking.
- **Record a few seconds of silence** at the start of each session. That room tone can help in the edit if you need to cover a gap.

## 5. Takes: give yourself useful footage

- **Do a test take first.** Record thirty seconds and watch it back before filming the real thing.
- **Leave a beat before and after you speak.** A second or two of stillness gives you clean edit points.
- **Film in sections.** For longer tutorials, recording one section at a time keeps your energy up and makes mistakes cheaper to redo.
- **Say the take name aloud.** "Video two, section three, take one" makes clips much easier to find later.
- **Record key lines twice.** If a line really matters, get a spare while you are still set up.

## 6. Review: check before you pack away

Check your test take carefully, then do a quicker check at the end of the session. Look for:

- Focus on your eyes, not the background.
- Framing that has not drifted.
- Consistent light and colour across takes.
- Clear audio with no distortion, hum or echo.

Note your best takes while they are fresh. Then write down one thing to change next time. That small habit is how a setup improves without buying more kit.

## Your repeatable checklist

1. Write your one-sentence message and choose the format.
2. Rebuild the frame from your tape marks and photo.
3. Face the light, then lock focus and exposure if you can.
4. Quieten the room, then test and listen to the audio.
5. Do a test take, then film in sections with a beat at each end.
6. Review, note your best takes and one improvement.
